ground_truth: Well, let me give you a little bit of his family background because oftentimes for all of us, the family experience that we have growing up as children is often when the values begin to get deep into our heart and mind. And it was certainly true in his case, as it is for each one of us here. We can have a tremendous sense of gratitude, even at the not-so-good things that happen in our family lives. We live in a day in which there's a lot of dysfunctional family. But my dad and my mom both grew up in a very dysfunctional family. My dad says that as he was growing up in the Great Depression, he was born in 1921 in Eaton, Georgia. We had this boll weevil and some other things that happened. We had the Great Depression back in the late 1920s, 28, 29, 30. And his father, who was the breadwinner of the family, was very discouraged. He was in real estate. He sold insurance. Nobody was buying policies. Land was not selling. And so he goes home to a wife and four daughters, three sons, and wasn't able to provide for the family. And it was very demeaning for him. I mean, the male role in the household at the time was that the males were the breadwinner of the family. And my dad growing up in that city, just how discouraging his father was. He could remember being beaten on the rear end with a razor. He could remember being raped and almost verbally abusive, if not physically abusive, right on the edge. However, it reminds us that we don't have to be a victim of our circumstances. That even through the not-so-good things that happened in our life, the background, are forged, you know, some values and truths. My dad said he could never remember his father ever saying he loved him. Now, that's almost unimaginable today for me. Because... Because my dad was so affirming in my life. He would... One of my favorite little sticky notes that I've got in my office at home was just a little 3M sticky note that just said, I love you, and his dad underneath it. And, you know, what a treasure that is for me. That affirmation that we get is part of building that character and value set in our life. It's a huge reminder to all of us who aspire to be parents. How important... How important those values are and how they begin to affect the lens through which we see the world and how we process and make choices and decisions. My mother, she came also from a dysfunctional family. Her father abandoned her when she was less than six months old. And she was raised by a single breadwinner mother who was a seamstress and did a lot of sewing. So, you know, the values that dad lived out were forged out of some not-so-good things that happened. And so, you know, I think that's one of the most important things that dad learned in his life. He had determination. He realized if he was going to have anything, he was going to have to go for it himself. It was not going to be an allowance or a stipend or anything else. He was going to have to go out there and earn it. So, he started selling Coca-Cola door-to-door. He discovered Earl Leonard. I don't know if he's here, but he's... The ghost of Earl Leonard is here. If he's not here, but he's with Coca-Cola, of course. But dad learned how to make a profit. He could buy a Coke for four cents. He could peddle it up down the street for five cents. If he added some ice to it and add a little value-add element to the raw cost of goods sold, he could make a profit. And once he tasted making a profit, he never wanted to go to earn a paycheck. I don't guess he was ever on anybody's payroll because he was always working for himself. But I think those early childhood experiences where we... It forges not only our way we make decisions, but also forges... How we view life and how we view the world in which we live. Absolutely.
